entry_audit.engineering_basis: Parameterized ambiguous silhouette; not a pixel-identical reproduction of a historical plate.
evidence_limitations: The generator verifies geometry and luminance, not bistable reports.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The entry instantiates a controllable ambiguous-figure stimulus family.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Equal central patches on unequal luminance surrounds.
evidence_limitations: Display calibration and observer adaptation are not modeled.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The physical center patches are matched while surround luminance differs.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Alternating rectangular masks at a fixed rational frame rate.
evidence_limitations: The artifact establishes temporal succession, not perceived motion.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The sequence contains controlled successive spatial events.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Additive octave-spaced partials with a deterministic envelope.
evidence_limitations: Playback transducers and listener pitch judgments are external.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The audio contains octave-related partials with controlled sweep parameters.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Harmonic components are synthesized while the nominal fundamental is omitted.
evidence_limitations: Pitch completion is an observer-level inference.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The nominal fundamental component is absent from the canonical spectrum.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: One flash paired with one or two timed beeps on a shared clock.
evidence_limitations: The stimulus does not establish a reported flash count.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The declared beep/flash event counts and offsets are physically encoded.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Stereo panning and visual displacement encode a spatial discrepancy.
evidence_limitations: Perceived localization depends on room, headphones, display, and observer.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The audio and visual channels carry a declared spatial discrepancy.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Equal bars with controlled arrow-wing geometry.
evidence_limitations: The chosen normalized geometry is one engineering variant.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The two bar lengths are equal in the canonical raster while wing geometry varies.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: A diagonal continuation is separated by a rectangular occluder.
evidence_limitations: Alignment judgments and orientation filters are not measured.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The occluder and diagonal continuation are generated from explicit geometry.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Equal target bars are placed inside converging rails.
evidence_limitations: Perspective interpretation is observer- and display-dependent.
entry_audit.supported_claim: Target bars are physically equal and rails converge toward a vanishing region.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Three incomplete circular inducers are rasterized around a triangular gap.
evidence_limitations: Illusory contour completion is not directly measured.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The image contains incomplete inducers with no explicitly drawn triangle edge.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Equal central targets are surrounded by different context-circle sizes.
evidence_limitations: Perceived size depends on viewing scale and context.
entry_audit.supported_claim: Central target geometry is held equal while contextual circle geometry differs.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Vertical long lines crossed by short oblique inducers with explicit normalized spacing and angle.
evidence_limitations: The raster verifies line geometry, not orientation judgments or a pixel-identical historical reproduction.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The entry instantiates a controlled crossing-line orientation stimulus family.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Two octave-complex tones are separated by a half-octave interval.
evidence_limitations: Ascending/descending reports vary across listeners and contexts.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The canonical pair has an explicit half-octave frequency relation.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Alternating high and low tones are assigned to opposite stereo channels.
evidence_limitations: The auditory percept depends on dichotic presentation and listener.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The two channels receive alternating octave-related tones.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: An interrupted sinusoidal carrier is replaced during a declared gap by a deterministic tone or white-noise masker with typed amplitude.
evidence_limitations: The generator reports the physical interruption and masker, not a listener's continuity judgment or sensory-versus-decisional effect.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The canonical audio contains a reproducible interruption interval and masker family.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: A visual flash and audio click share a clock with explicit offset.
evidence_limitations: The generated single-event pair is a simplified engineering stimulus.
entry_audit.supported_claim: Audio and video event timing and declared offset are deterministic and inspectable.

entry_audit.engineering_basis: Requires validated speech audio/video fixtures and licensing records.
evidence_limitations: No fixture, consent record, or perceptual validation contract is bundled.
entry_audit.missing_contract: A licensed or consented checksummed speech audio/video fixture, synchronization contract, and preregistered perceptual validation protocol are required.
entry_audit.supported_claim: The catalog identifies a speech-dependent audiovisual family without claiming implementation.

metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The Müller-Lyer effect, the apparent difference in the length of a line as the result of its adornment with arrowheads or arrow tails, is the best known and most controversial of the classical geometrical illusions. By sampling a range-image database of natural scenes, we show that the perceptual effects elicited by the MüllerLyer stimulus and its major variants are correctly predicted by the probability distributions of the possible physical sources underlying the relevant retinal images. These results support the conclusion that the Müller-Lyer illusion is a manifestation of the probabilistic strategy of visual processing that has evolved to contend with the uncertain provenance of retinal stimuli.</jats:p>

metadata.abstract: <jats:p>Max Wertheimer's 1912 monograph on apparent motion is a seminal contribution to the study of visual motion, but its actual contents are not widely known. This article attempts to clarify what the monograph did and did not contribute, emphasizing links between Wertheimer's principal findings and the results of subsequent investigations of motion perception, including currently active lines of research. The topics discussed include Wertheimer's experimental tests of explanations for apparent motion; his work with motion phenomena that lie between succession and optimum motion; his studies of the influence of attention on motion; explorations of various forms of hysteresis and motion transparency; and Wertheimer's work with a motion-blind patient.</jats:p>

metadata.abstract: <jats:p>A pattern of tones is explored that possesses some remarkable properties. It is heard as ascending when played in one key, yet as descending when played in another key. When the pattern is recorded on tape and then played back at different speeds, it is heard either as ascending or as descending depending on the speed of playback. As a further paradox, the pattern in any given key is heard as ascending by some listeners but as descending by others. Theoretical implications of these findings are discussed.</jats:p>
title: A Musical Paradox

metadata.abstract: <jats:p>Listeners were presented with a sequence of sinusoidal tones, each tone 250 msec in duration and with no gap between adjacent tones. All tones were either 400 or 800 Hz, and these frequencies were presented in strict alternation. This sequence of alternating tones presented at equal amplitude to both ears simultaneously for 20 sec. However, when one ear received 800 Hz, the other received 400 Hz and vice versa. Under these conditions 48% of 42 right-handed listeners perceived a single tone oscillating from ear to ear whose pitch also oscillated from one octave to the other in synchrony with the localization shift and with the higher pitch localized in the right ear. When the identical sequence was again presented but with earphones reversed, these listeners reported the identical percept with the higher pitch still localized in the right ear. Two listeners with absolute pitch identified the alternating pitches as G4 (392 Hz) and G5 (784 Hz). Another 14% of the listeners obtained the same illusion but with the high pitch consistently localized in the left ear. The remaining 38% reported a variety of percepts, but no listener perceived the stimulus correctly. A similar illusion also occurs with two frequencies arbitrarily chosen from within this octave range.</jats:p>

metadata.abstract: <jats:p>When an extraneous sound (such as a cough or tone) completely replaces a speech sound in a recorded sentence, listeners believe they hear the missing sound. The extraneous sound seems to occur during another portion of the sentence without interfering with the intelligibility of any phoneme. If silence replaces a speech sound, the gap is correctly localized and the absence of the speech sound detected.</jats:p>

metadata.abstract: <jats:p>In the present study, Jastrow's famous ambiguous drawing of a duck/rabbit was presented to 100 students along with 11 published variants from later research. The beak/ears of the animal pointed to the right for half of the subjects and to the left for the other half. For each figure subjects were required to rate the ease of bird and of rabbit identification on a 9-point scale. Raw data of subjects' ratings are presented for the convenience of experimenters planning research with a specific bird/rabbit figure. Of the 12 figures, 6 were significantly bird-dominant, 2 were rabbit-dominant, and only 4 figures were truly ambiguous, i.e., a bird was as easily identified as was a rabbit. With the exception of one figure (the whole-body representation of a duck/rabbit), bird and rabbit ratings were not affected by the orientation of the beak/ears. Jastrow's original drawing was the seventh out of the 12 figures in rated ambiguity, suggesting a secure place for it in research on visual ambiguity.</jats:p>

metadata.abstract: <jats:p>In previous studies of the ‘tritone paradox’ Deutsch has suggested that, when listeners are presented with pairs of octave-complex tones that are equal in average log frequency but differ in chroma by 6 semitones (a tritone), they perceive the direction of the chroma difference according to an individual pitch-class template. However, it has also been found that the perceived direction changes for many listeners when the spectral envelope of the tones is shifted along the frequency axis. Reanalysis of these data indicates a strong tendency to perceive the pitch class corresponding to the frequency on which the spectral envelope is centered as subjectively lowest. In experiment 1 this spectral-envelope effect was replicated with tone pairs presented in isolation, at the rate of one a day, which rules out artifacts of test format. In experiment 2, involving another context-free format, envelope center frequency was varied over a wide range and it was shown that some individuals are totally envelope dependent, whereas others rely more on pitch class, and yet others show mixed patterns. Experiment 3 demonstrated that listeners' judgments of tritone pairs can be swayed easily by preceding context. Finally, experiment 4 showed that strong envelope effects are also obtained with Deutsch's own tritone test (issued on CD). The subjective relative pitch height of octave-complex tones thus depends on several competing factors, only one of which is pitch class.</jats:p>

metadata.abstract: <jats:p>In a geometrical figure in which long vertical lines are each crossed by a series of short oblique lines, an illusory effect is obtained such that the orientations of the long lines are perceived as nonvertical and shifted away from the orientation of the oblique lines (the Zöllner illusion). In addition, the vertical separation between the crossing (oblique) lines is perceived as less than that if the crossing lines are horizontal (the Judd illusion). It has previously been shown that these two effects are closely related, and a single-process account has been proposed in which both effects are explained by a computational model involving band-pass spatial filtering of the figure by means of difference-of-Gaussians (DOG) filters. Two arguments are presented against the latter account. First, in an opposite-contrast-polarity figure with, for example, white vertical lines and black crossing lines on a mid-grey background, the peaks in the DOG filter output are such as to predict the reversal of the Zöllner—Judd effects. It is shown by demonstration that this prediction is disconfirmed, and that the normal effects are obtained. Second, it is shown that the normal Zöllner—Judd effects are obtained in the absence of the long vertical lines, and in the presence of anomalous contours. The latter effects are also in contradiction to the band-pass-filtering model. These findings are discussed in relation to a dual-process account of the Zöllner—Judd effects.</jats:p>

metadata.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>To form a coherent percept of the environment, the brain must integrate sensory signals emanating from a common source but segregate those from different sources. Temporal regularities are prominent cues for multisensory integration, particularly for speech and music perception. In line with models of predictive coding, we suggest that the brain adapts an internal model to the statistical regularities in its environment. This internal model enables cross‐sensory and sensorimotor temporal predictions as a mechanism to arbitrate between integration and segregation of signals from different senses.</jats:p>
